opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The Special Scholarship is often described as the highest honor for students at Tsinghua, and when I received it, I was grateful and a bit surprised. But looking back, I see it a little differently than I did at the time.

From the outside, people tend to treat it as a ranking, as if the recipients are the "best" students of that year. I don't think that's quite right. Each year there are many excellent people at Tsinghua who never apply, or whose work just isn't the kind that fits neatly into a ten-minute defense in front of a committee. So I see the scholarship as recognizing a certain kind of story: someone who has done solid work and can explain clearly why it matters.

For me, the most valuable part wasn't the title or the money. It was the process of preparing for it. You're forced to step back and ask: what have I actually done in these years? What's the thread connecting my research? Is it meaningful beyond publishing papers? That kind of reflection is rare when you're busy chasing deadlines.

There's also a risk, honestly. Once you get a label like that, people expect certain things from you, and you can start to expect them from yourself. You might feel pressure to keep producing work that looks impressive instead of work that's actually useful. I've tried to be careful about that. Later on I spent a lot of time on open-source systems work, which is less glamorous in academic terms. It's a lot of engineering, debugging, and community support. But I found it very rewarding because real people use it every day.

So my view is: it's a nice encouragement and a good moment to reflect, but it shouldn't define you. The award is about the past. What matters more is what you choose to do afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

I think the Special Scholarship means something different from the inside than it looks from the outside. From the outside it's the highest honor Tsinghua gives undergraduates, and people talk about it like a crown. When I actually received it, my honest feeling was more complicated than pride.

The first thing I'd say is that it's a recognition of a trajectory, not of a single achievement. The committee looks at what you've done over several years, and in my case that was mostly research work that started quite early, around my second year, when I joined a lab and started working on transfer learning and later on systems problems around machine learning. None of those individual papers felt like a big deal at the time. The scholarship made me look back and realize those small steps added up to something. That was useful, because when you're in the middle of research you mostly feel like you're failing.

The second thing is that it carries a kind of responsibility. Once you have that label, people assume you know what you're doing. I didn't, and in some ways I still don't. So I tried to treat it less as "I've arrived" and more as "now I owe the people who invested in me." My advisor, Mingsheng Long, spent an enormous amount of time on me as an undergraduate, and the scholarship was in part a reflection of his patience.

The third thing, and this is the part I say to younger students who ask me about it, is that you should not optimize for it. The students who chase it tend to collect activities. The students who end up receiving it usually did one thing deeply and let the rest follow. For me that one thing was writing code and running experiments until something worked. The honor came as a byproduct. If I had been thinking about the scholarship in year two, I probably would have made worse decisions.

And finally, I'd be honest that there's luck involved. Tsinghua has many students who work as hard as I did and who are just as capable. The selection is a snapshot, and a few things falling into place at the right time matters. I try to remember that whenever someone introduces me with it.

I’m grateful for the recognition, but I think the more important question is what you do afterward. You still have to choose meaningful problems, keep learning, and do the work. The scholarship is a milestone, rather than the goal itself.
